title: APT30
summary: APT30 is a tracking name for a long-running espionage cluster that public reporting links to China-nexus activity, with operations against government, diplomatic, military, and defence-industrial targets concentrated in South and Southeast Asia. The tradecraft described in public analyses is conventional but disciplined: spearphishing messages carrying malicious attachments or links, strategic website compromise to deliver implants, and modular backdoors that were reportedly customised per victim so that indicators rarely repeat across intrusions. In real environments the footprint shows up in mail-gateway logs, endpoint process ancestry, and outbound command-and-control traffic rather than in any single signature. The common misunderstanding is treating the label as a verified identity. APT30 is an analytic cluster name for shared infrastructure and tooling, attribution is asserted with varying confidence across vendors, and the group overlaps in reporting with other China-nexus labels, so defenders should track behaviour instead of the name.

beginner.definition: APT30 is a name used by security researchers for a long-running cyber spying group. Analysts believe it works for or with a state, and it mainly targets governments and militaries in Asia. The name is a research label, not a confirmed identity.
beginner.whyItMatters: This kind of group does not steal money. It steals plans, documents, and secrets, and it stays hidden for a long time. The attacks often start with a normal-looking email, so staff awareness matters. If you ignore quiet access, an intruder can sit in your network for months. Good logging and monitoring are how you find them.
howItWorks: The group studies its targets first, looking for staff who handle useful documents.
It sends a tailored email that looks like it comes from a trusted contact.
The message carries a harmful file, or it carries a link to a fake login page.
If the reader opens the file, hidden code runs and installs a small backdoor.
The backdoor quietly calls home to a server, and the attackers now have access.
They then move deeper into the network and copy the documents they came for.
beginner.example: Think of a night-shift security desk in a large office, where the guard only checks the main door. A visitor in a delivery uniform walks past with a clipboard and a name badge that looks right. Nobody stops him because he matches what staff expect to see. He spends hours inside, opens filing cabinets, and photographs documents. The guard never sees a break-in, because no door was forced. Spearphishing works the same way. The message looks normal, so the reader opens it without suspicion. The hidden program then gets in through the front door while nobody is watching.
takeaways: A research label like APT30 is not proof of who did it.
Most intrusions begin with one believable email to one person.
If you cannot see quiet access in your logs, you cannot stop it.

objectives: Explain what an advanced persistent threat is and why the label describes behaviour rather than a confirmed identity.
Describe how spearphishing and strategic website compromise deliver an initial foothold.
Identify the log sources that reveal a foothold, including mail gateways, endpoint process trees, and outbound network traffic.
Explain why per-victim customised malware makes signature-only detection unreliable.
Summarise how public reporting attributes APT30 and why that attribution carries differing confidence.
Describe defensive controls that reduce the value of a single phished endpoint.
